title: Equal pay and the marriage bar
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:52Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-04T17:58:52Z autoreview: cleared with the fix (remember other)

match.reason: Neither bank point teaches the Australian marriage bar ending in 1966 or the 1969 and 1972 equal pay decisions; the women's movement card only mentions equal pay as a general demand, and the interwar card only notes that women were expected to leave work on marriage, without the Australian legal detail.

draft.title: Equal pay and the marriage bar
card: a rule that forced women to leave federal public service jobs when they married. It was removed in 1966, so married women could keep their jobs.
pay set by the work done, not by the sex of the worker. Before the 1969 decision, women were often paid much less than men for the same work.
In 1969 the Conciliation and Arbitration Commission ruled for equal pay for equal work. This helped only women doing the same work as men.
In 1972 the Commission extended this to equal pay for work of equal value. Women in jobs that were mostly done by women could now be paid on the value of the work.
draft.remember: 1966 let married women keep their jobs. 1969 and 1972 moved pay towards the value of the work.

a.q: What did the removal of the marriage bar in 1966 change for women in the federal public service?
opts: Married women could keep their jobs
Women were paid the same as men
Women could be promoted to any job
Part-time work was open to all women
a.why: The marriage bar had forced women to leave when they married, so removing it let married women stay. It did not change pay. Equal pay came from the separate decisions of 1969 and 1972.
a.clue: The rule was about what happened when a woman married.

b.q: In 1970, Dana and Sam do the same job in a government office, but Dana is paid less because she is a woman. Which change would the 1969 decision have applied to her case?
opts: Equal pay, because the work was the same
Equal pay only if she was unmarried
Equal pay, because her job was of equal value
A pay rise only if she had worked longer
b.why: The 1969 decision set equal pay for equal work, and Dana and Sam do the same job. The idea of equal value came in 1972 and covered jobs that were different but worth the same. Marriage status was the issue of the marriage bar, not pay.
b.clue: Which decision dealt with the same work, not different jobs?

a.best: Married women could keep their jobs

b.best: Equal pay, because the work was the same

problems.detail: The remember line says both 1969 and 1972 'moved pay towards the value of the work'. The card draws a clear line between 1969 (equal pay for equal work, same jobs only) and 1972 (work of equal value). Grouping 1969 under 'value' blurs the very distinction question b tests.
